title: kv-cache-reuse-eviction-paging-memory-bandwidth-investigation-2026-08-12
content:
TL;DR:

We profiled KV-cache behavior across a set of representative workloads and identified two primary performance regimes: (1) cache-friendly requests where reuse is high and p95 latency is dominated by kernel execution, and (2) cache-miss/paging-heavy workloads where device-to-host or device-to-device memory transfers and memory bandwidth contention drive large p95 latency spikes. Key findings and recommendations: 

- Measured reuse rates vary widely by workload: small-chat workloads (avg seq 64) show >85% KV reuse for hot prefixes; long-context summarization (avg seq 2k) drops reuse to 15-30%.
- Eviction policy (current fixed-window LRU variant) induces thrashing under multi-tenant workloads with mixed sequence length, causing reuse oscillations and p95 latency tails.
- Paging (fallback to host-backed KV pages) occurs when per-GPU KV working set > ~48GB on A100-80GB; paging latency adds 20-200ms per request depending on access pattern.
- Measured sustained device memory bandwidth saturation on A100 during KV rehydration (reads) at ~780-820 GB/s of peak theoretical 1.0 TB/s (observed with microbenchmarks). This bandwidth pressure correlates with higher token-generation latency for co-hosted workloads.
- Recommendations: enable adaptive retention windows, introduce lightweight per-tenant working-set hints, prioritize KV prefetch for predicted-next-step tokens, and add NUMA/PCIe-aware placement for large-model KV pages. Short-term mitigations: lower default per-request max_cached_kv_bytes for mixed workloads, add a paging threshold alert, and add an opt-in experimental eviction policy (segmented LRU).

Background and motivation:

Our serving runtime uses an on-device KV cache to store attention key/value states across generation steps. Proper KV reuse is essential to reach target token-per-second throughput and low p50/p95 generation latency. Recent customer reports and internal SLO misses pointed to occasional long-tail latency regressions correlated with large-context generation and mixed workloads on the same GPU pool. This doc captures the experiments, profiling data, and proposed changes focused on reuse rates, eviction behavior, paging, and memory bandwidth interactions.

Workloads tested:

- chat-small: conversational stream, avg seq 48, batch sizes 1-8, hot prefixes from session cache (prod-like).
- summarization-long: single-turn long context, avg seq 2048, batch size 1, generates up to 512 tokens.
- instruction-mix: synthetic mix (30% small chat, 40% medium seq 256, 30% long seq 1024) to simulate multi-tenant tail behavior.
- microbench-kv: synthetic KV access patterns to isolate device memory bandwidth and rehydration costs.

Hardware and runtime config:

- Nodes: NVIDIA A100 80GB (PCIe) and H100 SXM in a staging pool (results below call out device).
- Runtime: serving-runtime v3.7.1-experimental with current KV cache impl (fixed-window LRU-ish) and default retention window 1024 steps.
- Compilation flags: optimized kernels enabled (FP16/AMP paths), heterogeneous kernel selection ON.
- Batching settings: dynamic batching enabled, batch timeout 10ms, max batch 32.

Methodology / instrumentation:

- Collected per-request traces with token-level timestamps (kv_read_start, kv_read_end, kernel_enqueue, token_emitted).
- Hardware counters: NVTX + nvprof style counters for PCIe transfers, cudaMemcpy times, and device memory throughput (nvidia-smi and CUPTI where available).
- Memory allocation sampling to detect host-backed page faults for KV areas (tracked via custom allocator events).
- Stress tests with microbench-kv to measure sequential/random read throughput and corresponding latency curves.

Key measurements and observations:

1) Reuse rates by workload (measured as fraction of KV hits for requested token steps):
- chat-small: median reuse 0.87, 95th reuse 0.74.
- summarization-long: median reuse 0.28, 95th reuse 0.12.
- instruction-mix: median reuse 0.52, 95th reuse 0.33.
Notes: reuse calculation excludes cached prefix hits that are satisfied by session-level prefix caching (we measure per-request KV lookup reuse).

2) Eviction patterns and thrashing:
- Under instruction-mix, eviction rate (evicted pages per minute per-GPU) increased 3x vs single-workload runs.
- Eviction oscillations observed: when a long-seq job starts, it forces eviction of frequently-used short-chat KV pages; when chat requests return, their reuse is low until pages are rehydrated, causing an elevated p95 for ~30-90s until steady-state.
- Current eviction policy does not differentiate by tenant or inferred "hotness" beyond recency window; this exposes multi-tenant workloads to adversarial-like thrashing.

3) Paging (host-device fallback) costs:
- Host-backed KV pages trigger synchronous device reads on first access (rehydration). Average rehydration latencies measured: 22ms (sequential read small pages), 120ms (random access across many pages) on A100 via PCIe. H100 shows lower rehydration 8-60ms depending on PCIe/NVLink topology.
- Paging is triggered when per-GPU KV allocated > ~48GB on A100-80GB (empirically observed threshold where allocator began using host slab). This aligns with our allocator's 80% soft limit + fragmentation overhead.

4) Memory bandwidth and co-tenancy impact:
- Microbench-kv sequential reads saturated device memory bandwidth up to ~820 GB/s on A100 (reported via CUPTI sampling), which caused kernel stalls and increased downstream token generation latencies by 15-40% for co-hosted kernels.
- Co-located workload interference: when a rehydration spike occurs for one tenant, other tenants on the same GPU experienced 10-50ms added tail latency depending on batch mix.

5) End-to-end latency impact (p50/p95 token generation):
- chat-small (no interference): p50 ~18ms/token, p95 ~42ms/token.
- summarization-long (paging observed): p50 ~28ms/token, p95 ~320ms/token (paging + eviction thrash observed).
- instruction-mix: p50 ~22ms/token, p95 ~160ms/token (transient spikes during mixed workload transitions).

Analysis and root causes:

- The primary drivers of long-tail latency are: (A) synchronous rehydration of host-backed KV pages over PCIe/NVLink, and (B) eviction-induced re-population of KV for hot prefixes in mixed-tenant pools. Both are amplified by memory bandwidth saturation: rehydration reads are device-memory heavy and compete with attention-kernel reads/writes.
- The fixed-window eviction policy is too coarse for mixed workloads; it lacks tenant affinity and working-set estimation, so it evicts frequently-accessed short-chat pages when a long job arrives.
- Fragmentation of device memory inflates the practical KV capacity (we see usable threshold < nominal 80GB due to fragmentation + fragmentation from other runtime allocations).

Recommendations (short/medium/long term):

Short-term (1-3 weeks):
- Lower default per-request max_cached_kv_bytes for multi-tenant pools to 40GB effective to avoid host paging threshold. (Config override in pool config).
- Add an alert when allocator uses host-backed KV pages for >1% of requests in a 5m window.
- Add telemetry for eviction oscillations: emit eviction and rehydration deltas per-tenant to detect thrash within 60s windows.
- Expose a per-deployment experimental flag: segmented-LRU (two-tier hot/cold cache) to reduce eviction of proven hot prefixes.

Medium-term (1-3 months):
- Implement working-set hinting: allow service-layer to attach an estimated per-session KV working set (bytes) so runtime can reserve/partition cache accordingly. Add a best-effort reservation mechanism.
- NUMA/PCIe-aware placement: prefer NVLink-local placement for rehydration-heavy workloads when available; schedule large-KV jobs on nodes with NVLink fabric that reduces PCIe penalties.
- Prefetch heuristic: for autoregressive flows, prefetch predicted-next-step KV pages for top-K likely continuation tokens to hide rehydration latency (costed via default budget).

Long-term (3-6 months):
- Implement tenant-aware eviction policy that combines recency + frequency + tenant-weighted reservations (segmented LFU variant).
- Explore compression-friendly KV layouts: compress cold KV pages to reduce device footprint and decompress on read with GPU kernels to minimize PCIe reads.
- Investigate GPU-side memory overcommit with async on-demand paging (requires allocator + driver cooperations), or move to HBM-coherent fabrics where possible.

Experiments to validate changes:

- Run 48-hour A/B with segmented-LRU flag on instruction-mix pool; measure p95 reduction and eviction rate. Success criterion: p95 reduction >= 40% for the 95th percentile without reducing median by >5%.
- Test working-set hints on 2 tenants with antagonistic patterns (one long, many short) to validate reservation prevents thrash. Success: eviction oscillation measured delta < 15% vs baseline.
- Microbench: simulate rehydration with and without prefetching to quantify latency savings vs extra memory bandwidth cost.

Open questions / unknowns:

- What is the safe default reservation fraction for per-tenant hints that balances overall utilization vs thrash protection?
- How effectively can compression help without adding decompression CPU/GPU latency that negates benefits?
- For H100 NVLink topologies, can we rely on reduced rehydration latencies to relax some paging thresholds? Need more H100-focused runs.

Appendix (artifacts and traces):

- Attached traces: nvtx_traces/investigation-2026-08-10.zip (contains per-request timelines and CUPTI counters).
- Flamegraphs: flamegraphs/rehydration-seq-2048.svg, flamegraphs/segmented-lru-test.svg (see linked Confluence page).
- Microbench scripts: https://github.com/redwood-inference/serving-runtime/tree/main/bench/microbench-kv (PR 789).

Next steps (owner: Asha Patel):

- (week 1) Ship paging-usage alert + eviction telemetry (low-risk).
- (week 2) Land segmented-LRU experimental flag behind config and run 48h A/B on staging pools with instruction-mix. (owner: Miguel Santos)
- (month 1) Design working-set hint API and add API/SDK doc for partners to opt-in. (owner: Lina Zhou)

Notes to self / rough todos:

- Validate fragmentation heuristics; add allocator-level sampling to quantify fragmentation overhead.
- Validate H100 results (need access to 4-node NVLink cluster for representative runs).
- Discuss with infra about offering a "large-KV" node pool with higher eviction threshold and stricter tenant isolation for premium customers.

If you want, I can extract actionable JIRA tickets from the recommendations and open them, plus prepare a short slide deck for Eng Exec with the p95 impact charts.
